title: Interfaces: a promise
summary: An interface lists methods; implements is a class promising to have them.

say.never: A wall charger doesn't care whether you plug in a phone, a tablet or headphones. It only needs the thing to *be chargeable*. In Java that idea is an **interface**: a list of methods with no code inside them. It says "anything that signs up will have these methods".
say.bit: An **interface** lists methods with no bodies. It's a promise: every class that signs up will have these methods.

steps.title: In your lesson: A promise, not a class

say.never: `PowerUser` is the promise for this lesson: anything that draws current from the battery has a name and an amount of amps. Each method ends with a semicolon instead of `{ }`, because the interface doesn't say *how*, only *what*.

A class signs the promise with `implements`. Now it *has to* write every method the interface lists, or Java won't compile it. `@Override` on each one tells Java "this is one of the promised methods", so a typo in the name becomes an error instead of a silent bug.
say.bit: `implements Chargeable` signs the promise. The class must write every listed method; mark each with `@Override`.

steps.title: In your lesson: Signing up with implements

say.never: `Motor` signs up with `implements PowerUser`, then keeps the promise by writing `getName()` and `getAmps()`. They just hand back the fields the constructor already filled in.
say.bit: `Motor implements PowerUser` and writes both methods, returning its fields.

say.never: Here's the payoff. A variable of type `Chargeable` can hold headphones, a phone or anything else that signed up, and you can call the promised methods on it without knowing which one it really is.
say.bit: A `Chargeable` variable can hold any class that implements it.
